items.title: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
items.tldr: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims to have used a non‑public version of the Claude chatbot to produce a 250,000‑line Lean proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics. Verification by the community, including Fields medallist Terence Tao, will take months. The announcement coincides with Anthropic’s stock‑market debut, raising questions about timing, credibility, and the broader impact of AI‑driven mathematical discovery.
items.background: The Riemann hypothesis, posed in 1859, asserts a precise distribution of the non‑trivial zeros of the zeta function and underpins much of modern number theory and cryptography. For decades it has resisted proof despite intense effort. In 2024‑2025, large language models (LLMs) from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic began claiming breakthroughs on long‑standing problems such as the Navier‑Stokes equations and dozens of Olympiad‑level conjectures. These claims have sparked debate over verification standards, the role of human oversight, and whether commercial AI labs are using high‑profile mathematics as a marketing lever. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7, a proprietary LLM, was the tool Alpöge employed over six weeks, producing a formal proof in Lean, a proof‑assistant language that enables machine‑checked verification.

analysis.heading: Credibility and Verification Dynamics
analysis.content: The proof’s length — over 250,000 lines of Lean code — makes manual audit impractical; verification will rely on a combination of automated proof‑checking and human expert review. Terence Tao’s cautious endorsement highlights a new collaborative model: a human author (Alpöge) can guide reviewers through the AI‑generated structure, unlike earlier OpenAI releases where no human intermediary was identified. However, the timing — announced the day after Anthropic’s IPO — fuels skepticism about whether the claim is a genuine scientific milestone or a strategic publicity stunt. The community’s response will set a precedent for how future AI‑generated proofs are evaluated, especially regarding transparency of the model version, training data, and prompt engineering used.

analysis.heading: Commercial Incentives vs. Scientific Norms
analysis.content: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google are racing to demonstrate that their LLMs can tackle "grand challenges" in mathematics, physics, and computer science. Publicly announcing solutions before peer review serves marketing and investor relations, as evidenced by the stock‑listing coincidence. A group of senior mathematicians warned that such "boasting" threatens the integrity of mathematics by conflating computational output with rigorous proof. The tension mirrors earlier debates over AI‑generated art and literature, but the stakes are higher because mathematical proofs underpin cryptographic security, algorithmic complexity theory, and scientific modelling. Policy makers may need to consider disclosure requirements for AI‑assisted discoveries, akin to clinical‑trial registration.

analysis.heading: Implications for Agentic AI and Formal Verification
analysis.content: Alpöge’s workflow — iteratively prompting a non‑public Claude model, refining Lean statements, and assembling a massive proof script — exemplifies an emerging "agentic AI" paradigm where LLMs act as semi‑autonomous research assistants. The success of this approach could accelerate formal verification in software engineering, hardware design, and safety‑critical systems, where Lean and Coq are already used. Yet the reliance on proprietary, opaque models raises reproducibility concerns: other researchers cannot replicate the exact reasoning path without access to the same model version. Open‑source alternatives (e.g., Hugging Face’s LLaMA‑based math‑tuned models) may democratise the capability, but they currently lag behind the performance of closed‑source Opus‑class systems.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical and Regulatory Outlook
analysis.content: If AI‑driven proofs become routine, nations may treat advanced mathematical capability as a strategic asset, similar to quantum computing. Export controls on frontier models, data‑center localisation, and talent retention could become policy levers. The EU’s AI Act and the U.S. Executive Order on AI safety already hint at classification of "high‑impact" AI systems; a verified Riemann proof would likely trigger a reassessment of what constitutes a "dual‑use" capability. International bodies such as the International Mathematical Union may need to establish certification standards for AI‑assisted proofs to preserve trust across borders.

key_facts: Levent Alpöge, an Anthropic mathematician, claims a full Lean proof of the Riemann hypothesis generated with a non‑public Claude Opus 4.7 model over six weeks.
The proof comprises >250,000 lines of Lean code; verification by experts including Terence Tao is expected to take months.
Announcement coincided with Anthropic’s U.S. stock‑market debut, prompting timing criticism.
OpenAI previously claimed AI‑assisted progress on Navier‑Stokes and 372 other problems, none yet peer‑reviewed.
A collective of mathematicians warned that premature commercial claims jeopardise mathematical rigor.
implications: Verification pipelines will need hybrid human‑AI review frameworks, potentially standardised by bodies like the IMU.
Commercial AI labs may face pressure to disclose model versions, training data, and prompt logs for high‑profile claims.
Agentic AI workflows could reshape formal methods in software/hardware verification, but proprietary access limits reproducibility.
Governments may classify advanced math‑capable LLMs as strategic technologies, influencing export‑control regimes.
items.outlook: The next 6‑12 months will be decisive: if the Lean proof withstands community scrutiny, it will mark the first AI‑verified solution to a Millennium Prize problem, catalysing a wave of AI‑assisted formal mathematics and prompting regulatory frameworks for high‑impact AI discoveries. Failure or prolonged ambiguity will reinforce skepticism and may slow commercial incentives for grand‑challenge claims.

items.fulltext:
In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
- Published
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent AlpÃ¶ge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. AlpÃ¶ge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
AlpÃ¶ge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," AlpÃ¶ge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete proof that AlpÃ¶ge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 lines long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.
A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

items.title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
items.tldr: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced a new EU‑UK agreement covering food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme, and signalled a willingness to pursue deeper integration beyond the current Parliament.
items.background: The agreement, finalised in Brussels on Friday, represents the latest stage of the post‑Brexit "reset" begun under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer. It removes most sanitary and phytosanitary checks on British food exports from 2028 in exchange for the UK aligning with a subset of EU regulations. A reciprocal youth experience scheme will permit up to 100,000 EU citizens aged 18‑31 to live, work and study in the UK for up to three years, with an equivalent quota for Britons in the EU, targeting launch by January 2030. The two sides also concluded talks on linking their emissions trading systems, aiming for implementation in 2028, and pledged closer cooperation on migrant smuggling and data sharing between law‑enforcement agencies. The Treasury estimates the package could add up to £17 billion annually to UK GDP, a figure contested by opposition leaders.

analysis.heading: Economic Impact and Trade‑offs
analysis.content: The Treasury’s £17 bn projection rests on reduced non‑tariff barriers for agri‑food exporters and the anticipated efficiency gains from a linked carbon market. However, critics note that the UK will become a "rule taker" on food standards from 2028, limiting regulatory autonomy. The youth scheme could alleviate labour shortages in hospitality and tech, yet the tuition‑fee negotiation remains a potential stumbling block that could diminish the scheme’s attractiveness for EU students. Independent analysts from the Institute for Fiscal Studies caution that the macro‑economic boost assumes full utilisation of the new market access and does not account for possible friction in regulatory alignment.

analysis.heading: Political Reactions and Domestic Constraints
analysis.content: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch dismissed the deal as unfair, arguing that British farmers will be bound by Brussels‑made rules while more EU youths compete for scarce entry‑level jobs. Reform UK’s Nigel Farage labelled the agreement a "betrayal" and a humiliation of the 2016 referendum result. Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey welcomed the youth mobility element but insisted that only a comprehensive new deal — including customs cooperation and services market access — would deliver meaningful growth. Prime Minister Burnham’s commitment to the 2024 manifesto pledge of no return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement constrains the depth of any future integration, forcing the government to pursue incremental, sector‑specific agreements.

analysis.heading: Strategic Outlook for EU‑UK Relations
analysis.content: Both Burnham and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the summit as a "turning point" and agreed to an informal "brainstorming process" before the next EU‑UK summit to explore long‑term options. This suggests a shift from transactional deals to a strategic dialogue that could eventually encompass defence, energy security and digital regulation. The 10‑year plan due next month will likely frame reindustrialisation and regional growth as domestic imperatives that are "connected to our long‑term relationship with our nearest partner." However, the next general election, required by August 2029, means any deepening beyond the current Parliament will need a fresh electoral mandate, making the upcoming brainstorming a pre‑campaign positioning exercise.

key_facts: Deal removes most checks on UK food exports from 2028 in return for regulatory alignment.
Youth experience scheme allows 100,000 EU and UK young people each to live, work, study for up to three years, targeting January 2030 launch.
Emissions trading systems to be linked from 2028.
Treasury estimates up to £17 bn annual GDP boost; opposition disputes the figure.
Legislation to implement the agreement expected in UK Parliament next week.
implications: UK agri‑food sector gains market access but loses regulatory sovereignty on standards.
Youth mobility may ease labour shortages but tuition‑fee dispute could limit participation.
Linked carbon markets create a precedent for deeper climate policy coordination.
Political opposition frames the deal as a breach of Brexit promises, potentially energising Eurosceptic voters.
Brainstorming process signals willingness to explore broader integration, contingent on electoral outcome.
items.outlook: The immediate focus will be on parliamentary ratification and operationalising the youth scheme and emissions link. Over the next 12‑18 months the informal brainstorming will test appetite for a more ambitious framework — possibly a veterinary agreement, mutual recognition of professional qualifications, or a security‑defence pact. The trajectory will hinge on the 2029 election result; a Labour‑led government may pursue deeper alignment, while a Conservative or Reform‑led administration could halt or reverse the current momentum.
items.fulltext:
UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
- Published
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to Â£17bn a year.
European Council President AntÃ³nio Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.
The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.
The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.
A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.
There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.
- Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more 
  - Published8 hours ago
- What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? 
  - Published8 hours ago
- Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow 
  - Published8 hours ago
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."
On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.
Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".
The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.
'Brainstorming process'
Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."
The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.
Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".
He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.
Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.
"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.
The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.
Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".
'Endless betrayal'
Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".
Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "Â£17bn boost to the British economy".
She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".
Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."
In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."
